passage: Every morning at the dairy cooperative outside Karad, the testing line backed up because each sample was logged on paper twice. The women waiting with their cans grumbled; the senior clerks shrugged, "Always been this way." Tushar, eight months into the job, had timed it for two weeks in a notebook: about forty minutes lost daily, most of it copying. He didn't raise it at the Monday meeting, where the manager, Yusuf-bhai, always turned defensive in front of the board members. He waited for a quiet Thursday afternoon, knocked, and laid the notebook on the desk. "Bhai, we both want the farmers home before the heat. One register instead of two would save most of this." Yusuf-bhai read slowly and frowned. "The auditors like two." "Then maybe a trial for one week, just on the evening shift?" A long pause. "One week. Evening only." Less than Tushar had hoped. Still, a start.

qa.q: How much time did Tushar find was lost each day?
qa.a: About forty minutes lost daily, most of it copying.

qa.q: Why did Tushar wait for a quiet Thursday instead of the Monday meeting?
qa.a: He was wary that Yusuf-bhai would turn defensive in front of the board members, and hoped a private talk would feel less threatening.

qa.q: Which parts of Tushar's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: He brought two weeks of timed facts, spoke privately, and framed it around getting farmers home before the heat, so it sounded like a shared goal.

qa.q: How might Yusuf-bhai see Tushar's suggestion?
qa.a: He may feel cautious because the auditors like two registers, yet respected enough by the calm, factual approach to allow a small trial.

grounding: Shows a young employee raising a problem privately with facts framed around a shared goal, and accepting slow change.

passage: You're asking if leaving means failing, Salma? Let your Sharmila Khala tell you something. At twenty-five I worked at a big export house in Tiruppur. Good job, and a boss who made us sign quality papers for batches we had never checked. Everyone signed. My friend Revathi said, "Close your eyes, it's how things are done." For months I shrank. I stopped laughing at lunch. I stopped telling my mother anything about work. One night I sat with a notebook and wrote two columns: what staying was costing me, and what leaving would cost. The first column was longer. I didn't storm out. I found another job, finished my pending orders, trained the girl who replaced me, and left with a proper letter. Revathi didn't speak to me for a month. Two years later, she left too.

qa.q: What were the workers made to sign?
qa.a: They signed quality papers for batches they had never checked.

qa.q: What does young Sharmila's shrinking show she was feeling?
qa.a: She was unhappy and uneasy, slowly losing herself; she stopped laughing at lunch and stopped telling her mother about work.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why was her way of leaving wise?
qa.a: Writing the two columns showed that staying cost more; she then found another job and finished her work first, so she left with dignity.

qa.q: Why might Revathi have stopped speaking to Sharmila for a month?
qa.a: Revathi may have felt judged or left behind, since the leaving questioned the habit Revathi had accepted.

grounding: Sharmila Khala recalls weighing a workplace whose values she could not live with and planning a calm, dignified exit.

passage: In the block agriculture office at Sehore, favours moved like small coins. Pankaj was a master of them: a leave form signed early here, the jeep lent there, every kindness remembered and quietly collected. Ritu did something duller. If she said the soil reports would reach the villages by Friday, they reached by Friday. When the pest survey went well, she read out the names of the two field assistants who had walked the fields. When canteen talk turned to the new officer's family, she finished her tea and left. So when the district team asked who should lead the new seed trial, the room went quiet, and then the head clerk said, "Ritu. Her dates are real." Pankaj laughed, a little tightly. "I've done more people more favours." "Yes," said the clerk. "That's why they owe you. They trust her."

qa.q: By when did Ritu say the soil reports would reach the villages?
qa.a: By Friday, and they reached by Friday.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have felt when the head clerk chose Ritu?
qa.a: He was probably stung and a little jealous; the tight laugh suggests he expected his favours to count for more.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's habits built her influence, and why?
qa.a: Keeping her dates, naming the field assistants who did the work, and leaving gossip behind made people trust her without owing her anything.

qa.q: How might the two field assistants see Ritu after the pest survey?
qa.a: They likely feel valued and loyal, because she gave them credit in front of everyone instead of keeping it.

grounding: Shows a colleague whose reliability, credit to others and distance from gossip earn quiet influence that outlasts favours.

subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]
passage: Trisha, you asked why I let you come to Rukmini Aunty's prayer meeting. Let your Manoj Nana tell you about when I was eight. My Dadi died one winter, and the whole house changed overnight. My father, who never cried, sat on the floor with his head on his knees. My aunts wept in the kitchen. And everyone kept sending me outside to play. "He's too small," they said. I wasn't too small. I knew. I sat on the front steps and felt like the only one in the house without a job. Then my mother came out, took my hand and said, "Come, help me put flowers near her photo. Dadi liked marigolds." I cried then, properly, with all of them. So yes, beta, you come. You'll see us cry, and that is allowed.

qa.q: What flowers did Dadi like?
qa.a: Dadi liked marigolds.

qa.q: How did young Manoj feel while sitting on the front steps?
qa.a: He felt shut out and lonely, like the only one without a job in a grieving house, even though he understood what had happened.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped young Manoj, and why?
qa.a: His mother included him by asking him to put flowers near Dadi's photo, which gave him an honest part in the grief and let him cry with the family.

qa.q: Why might the adults have kept sending Manoj outside to play?
qa.a: They probably wanted to shield a small child from their crying, not realising that being sent away made him feel more alone.

grounding: Manoj Nana recalls seeing adults grieve as a child, and how being included simply and honestly helped more than being shielded.

subtype: Joy of festival and team victory [Actor]
passage: The whistle blew, and the school gym exploded. Chandrika hadn't even played in the kabaddi final; she had only carried the water bottles. But when Jyoti, the team's smallest raider, slipped back over the line with the last point, Chandrika found herself screaming until her throat hurt. Sixth graders she had never spoken to were hugging her. The PT teacher, Mr Thomas, was jumping like a kid. Someone started the school song, badly, and three hundred voices joined in. Chandrika sang the wrong words and didn't care at all. On the bus home she kept touching the paper medal Jyoti had pressed into her hand. "It's everyone's," Jyoti had said. For once, it really felt that way.

qa.q: What was Chandrika's job at the kabaddi final?
qa.a: She had only carried the water bottles.

qa.q: Why was Chandrika screaming even though she hadn't played?
qa.a: She felt a huge shared joy and pride in the team's win, bigger than her own small part in it.

qa.q: How did Jyoti help others feel part of the win?
qa.a: By pressing the paper medal into Chandrika's hand and saying it was everyone's, Jyoti shared the victory instead of keeping it.

qa.q: What might the win have felt like for Jyoti, the raider who scored the last point?
qa.a: Jyoti was likely thrilled and relieved, and wanted the helpers on the side to share the moment too.

grounding: Shows a child in a school crowd celebrating a team win and feeling a joy bigger than her own, part of something shared.

passage: The news came on Tuesday morning in the school hall in Utrecht: Jonas from 10B had died in a cycling accident at the weekend. Nobody moved. Then Leila began to cry, loudly, into her sleeve. Two boys at the back cracked a joke and laughed too hard, then went red. Emil just stared at the floor. He kept thinking of the pencil Jonas had lent him in September, still in his case, and that he had never said thanks. At lunch the canteen was strangely polite. Someone snapped at the jokers, "Have some respect." The counsellor, Ms de Vries, spoke quietly to the tables. "People grieve in different ways. Crying, joking, going silent. None of that is wrong. My door is open all week." Emil went on Thursday, holding the pencil.

qa.q: What had Jonas lent Emil in September?
qa.a: Jonas had lent him a pencil in September.

qa.q: Why did Emil keep thinking about the pencil?
qa.a: He felt guilty and sad that he had never said thanks, and the pencil made the loss feel personal.

qa.q: How did Ms de Vries support a school grieving in so many ways?
qa.a: She said openly that crying, joking and silence are all normal, and offered an open door all week, so students like Emil could come when ready.

qa.q: Why might the two boys at the back have laughed too hard?
qa.a: They were probably shocked and awkward, and the laughter was a nervous way of coping, which is why they went red afterwards.

grounding: Shows a whole school hit by a classmate's death, with students crying, joking or going silent, and none of it treated as wrong.

passage: Rain drove the school's annual day into the cramped assembly hall, and the noise doubled: drums, whistles, the Class 11 dance crew shrieking about costumes. Tenzin stood by the back wall holding the sound cables he had promised to manage. Three weeks ago his Momo-la had died, and he had come back to school early because staying home was worse. Now everyone was so happy it felt like a wall he couldn't climb. When the whole hall sang for the principal's birthday, he mouthed the words and felt lonelier than he had at the cremation. Avni, from the dance crew, came over with a paper plate of jalebis. She didn't say "cheer up". She just stood beside him, held the other end of the cable, and stayed until the lights went off.

qa.q: Why was the annual day held in the assembly hall?
qa.a: Rain drove it into the cramped assembly hall.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel while the hall sang for the principal?
qa.a: He felt lonelier than at the cremation; everyone's happiness felt like a wall between him and them.

qa.q: Why did Avni's approach help more than telling Tenzin to cheer up?
qa.a: She stayed beside him and shared his task without asking him to feel happy, so he had company in his sadness.

qa.q: How might the celebration look to the dance crew?
qa.a: To them it is a noisy, exciting day, and most probably don't notice that the same noise is painful for someone grieving.

grounding: Shows a grieving teenager watching a school celebration and feeling doubly alone, as shared joy sharpens his sorrow.

passage: You asked why I went, even though I'm not a candle person. I'm Kiran, and honestly I didn't know what to do with any of it. Dr Nirmala Rao taught us statistics for two years, and then one Monday she was just gone. That evening about two hundred of us stood on the library steps. Someone handed me a candle. We didn't speak much. We sang the college song, slowly, and then the old film song she used to hum while marking. I don't sing. I sang. My hands stopped shaking once they had the candle to hold. When we set the candles down in rows, it looked like the lines on her graphs. I couldn't have made a speech that night. But I could light a wick like everyone else, and that was enough to carry it home.

qa.q: Where did the students gather that evening?
qa.a: They stood on the library steps.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel once the candle was in hand?
qa.a: Kiran felt steadier and comforted; the shaking stopped once there was something to hold and do alongside the others.

qa.q: Why might shared acts help when words fail, as they did for Kiran?
qa.a: Doing the same simple things as everyone, lighting, singing, placing candles, gave shape to grief that Kiran could not have put into a speech.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran had stayed away from the vigil?
qa.a: Kiran would likely have carried the loss alone, without the comfort of standing with two hundred others who felt it too.

grounding: Kiran finds comfort in a college vigil, where doing the same acts as others gives shape to grief without words.

subtype: Noticing a friend not joining in [Observer]
passage: At the Holi gathering in the lane behind the Pandharpur temple, everyone was pink and shrieking. Irawati, colour in her hair, noticed Kishore on the steps of the grain shop, shirt still clean, turning a steel glass of thandai in his hands. Last year he had been the first to throw colour. His cousins waved at him; he waved back and didn't move. Someone yelled, "Kishore, come on, don't be boring!" Irawati wiped her hands on her dupatta and sat on the step beside him, not too close. "Too much noise today?" she asked. He shrugged. "Baba's not well. Didn't feel like it." "Okay," she said. "I'll sit here a bit." She didn't dab colour on him. After a while, he tipped a little green onto her palm himself.

qa.q: What was Kishore holding on the steps?
qa.a: He was turning a steel glass of thandai in his hands.

qa.q: What was Irawati thinking when she noticed Kishore's clean shirt?
qa.a: She was concerned, because he had been the first to throw colour last year, and she sensed something was wrong.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's way of checking in work?
qa.a: She asked one gentle question, accepted his answer, and sat with him without pushing colour or cheer on him, so he could join in at his own pace.

qa.q: What might the shout of "don't be boring" have felt like for Kishore?
qa.a: It probably felt heavy and lonely, as if his worry about Baba had to be hidden to please the crowd.

grounding: Irawati notices a friend quiet in the middle of Holi and checks in softly without pushing him to feel happy.

subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: In the hospital family room, the morning after Sachin's father died, three people grieved in three directions. Sachin's younger brother, Nikhil, was on the phone nonstop: the crematorium, the priest, the relatives in Indore, a list growing on his palm in blue ink. Nazia, Sachin's wife, kept trying to talk. "Remember how he sang in the car?" she said, twice. Sachin sat by the window and said nothing. Inside, he was furious with both of them. How could Nikhil think about timings? Why did Nazia need words? Around noon Nikhil snapped, "Could you at least help, bhaiya?" Sachin nearly shouted back. Then he saw his brother's hands shaking over the list. He took the phone. "You call the family. I'll call the priest." Later, in the corridor, he told Nazia, "I can't talk yet. Stay close anyway?" She nodded and held his arm.

qa.q: What was Nikhil writing on his palm?
qa.a: A list of calls, the crematorium, the priest and the relatives in Indore, growing on his palm in blue ink.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling as he sat by the window?
qa.a: He was grieving silently and also angry, judging Nikhil for thinking about timings and Nazia for needing words.

qa.q: What helped the three of them grieve side by side?
qa.a: Sachin noticed Nikhil's shaking hands and shared the calls, and told Nazia plainly that he couldn't talk yet but wanted her close.

qa.q: How might Nazia have seen Sachin's silence?
qa.a: She may have felt shut out and worried that he was not grieving at all, until he explained and asked her to stay close.

grounding: Shows one family grieving in different styles, quiet, talking and keeping busy, where understanding each style reduces hurt.
